topicName: Daemon Crash Recovery and Disk Cleanup
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Daemon Crash Recovery and Disk Cleanup in Docker"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Docker is an essential tool for containerized environments, but unexpected daemon crashes can lead to corrupted states, locked volumes, and lingering disk bloat. This tutorial covers how to safely recover from a Docker daemon crash and perform comprehensive disk cleanups."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Docker Daemon Crashes"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When the Docker daemon (dockerd) crashes abruptly due to an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer, kernel panic, or host reboot, it can leave runtime locks on the filesystem. Containers might appear stuck in a 'Stopping' or 'Dead' state."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 1: Diagnosing the Daemon State"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before attempting recovery, check the system logs to identify the root cause of the daemon failure using systemctl or journalctl."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"sudo journalctl -u docker.service --since \"1 hour ago\""},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 2: Restarting and Repairing the Daemon"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"If the daemon fails to start automatically, you need to manually stop any lingering container processes, clear stale PID files, and restart the service."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"sudo systemctl stop docker\nsudo rm -f /var/run/docker.pid\nsudo systemctl start docker"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"If the storage driver is locked or corrupted, you may need to check `/var/lib/docker` for consistency. Avoid deleting files in this directory manually unless instructed by official Docker support."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 3: Comprehensive Disk Cleanup"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Crashes often leave behind dangling images, unused volumes, and stopped containers that consume valuable disk space. Docker provides a built-in command to prune unused data safely."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"docker system prune -a --volumes"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The -a flag removes all unused images, not just dangling ones."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The --volumes flag ensures that unused volumes associated with stopped containers are also purged."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 4: Advanced Cleanup for Persistent Storage Leaks"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Sometimes overlay2 storage drivers accumulate stale layers that standard pruning misses. You can inspect disk usage specifically to find leaks."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"docker system df -v"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"To clean up orphaned build cache which frequently bloats after frequent crashes or failed CI/CD pipelines, execute the following command:"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"docker builder prune -a"},{"order":22,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"By following these steps, you can successfully recover a corrupted Docker daemon state and reclaim disk space. Regular automated pruning via cron jobs can also prevent disk exhaustion issues in production environments."}]
